# Investigation Report: 2023 3CX DesktopApp Software Supply-Chain Compromise

## Executive assessment

The strongest public evidence indicates that the 2023 compromise of the 3CX DesktopApp was not initiated inside 3CX by exploiting the application’s customers. Instead, the intrusion into 3CX appears to have begun when a 3CX employee’s computer acquired a maliciously modified version of Trading Technologies’ X_TRADER application. That earlier compromise provided the threat actor with an entry point into the 3CX corporate environment. The actor then harvested credentials, moved laterally, compromised both Windows and macOS build environments, and inserted malicious code into legitimate 3CX DesktopApp installers. Those installers were subsequently distributed to 3CX customers as signed software updates. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

The public evidence supports a high-confidence reconstruction of the technical sequence but only a qualified attribution. Mandiant tracked the activity as **UNC4736**, a “suspected North Korean nexus cluster,” and assessed with moderate confidence that UNC4736 was related to financially motivated North Korean **AppleJeus** activity. Kaspersky independently associated the Gopuram payload and related infrastructure with **Lazarus** with medium-to-high confidence. MITRE ATT&CK records AppleJeus as software used by Lazarus Group. Accordingly, the most defensible public characterization is that the operation was attributed to a North Korea-linked activity cluster associated with UNC4736, AppleJeus, and the broader Lazarus Group umbrella, while recognizing that these labels are assessments rather than independently proven identities. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise); [Kaspersky, 2023](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/); [MITRE ATT&CK, 2025](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0584/))

The incident is especially significant because it publicly established a cascading supply-chain compromise: one software supply-chain attack involving Trading Technologies enabled a second supply-chain attack involving 3CX. Mandiant stated that this was the first such chain it had identified with concrete evidence. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

## Scope and source assessment

This report uses only the supplied source material. The sources differ in purpose and evidentiary value:

| Source | Evidentiary contribution | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Mandiant/Google Cloud | Intrusion reconstruction, malware analysis, build-environment compromise, cluster assessment | Primary technical investigation and most authoritative source for the chain |
| Kaspersky Securelist | Gopuram deployment, victim targeting, Lazarus linkage, file paths and hashes | Independent technical telemetry and attribution evidence |
| Google TAG | Earlier AppleJeus activity and compromise of Trading Technologies’ website | Historical infrastructure and campaign context |
| MITRE ATT&CK | Structured relationship between AppleJeus and Lazarus Group | Useful corroborative knowledge base, not a case-specific incident report |
| Cyber Security Agency of Singapore | Affected versions, capabilities, and defensive advice | Government advisory confirming operational impact |
| WIRED | Public synthesis of Mandiant’s findings and cryptocurrency-targeting hypothesis | Secondary reporting; useful for context, but less authoritative than Mandiant |
| Cybersecurity Dive | Early reporting on detection, scale, affected platforms, and suspected actor | Early situational reporting; some details were later refined |

The Mandiant report is prioritized because it describes direct incident-response findings from the 3CX environment, including the initial intrusion vector and compromise of the build systems. Kaspersky’s independent telemetry is important because it identifies post-compromise Gopuram deployments and provides separate attribution indicators. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise); [Kaspersky, 2023](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

## Reconstructed public evidence chain

### 1. Earlier compromise of Trading Technologies’ X_TRADER software

Mandiant identified a malicious software package distributed through the Trading Technologies website as the initial compromise vector into 3CX. The package was a tampered X_TRADER installer named `X_TRADER_r7.17.90p608.exe`, with MD5 hash `ef4ab22e565684424b4142b1294f1f4d`. Mandiant reported that the installer was digitally signed with the subject “Trading Technologies International, Inc.” and contained a signed `Setup.exe`. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

The X_TRADER installer deployed a modular backdoor called **VEILEDSIGNAL**. The loading chain used two malicious DLLs, a benign executable for DLL side-loading, and publicly available components named **SIGFLIP** and **DAVESHELL**. SIGFLIP decrypted an embedded payload using RC4, while DAVESHELL loaded the resulting payload into memory. VEILEDSIGNAL supported commands to send implant data, execute shellcode, and terminate itself. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

Mandiant found technical similarities between the compromised X_TRADER package and the later 3CX malware. These included:

- Reuse of the RC4 key `3jB(2bsG#@c7`;
- Use of SIGFLIP;
- Use of DAVESHELL;
- The hard-coded cookie variable `__tutma`;
- AES-256-GCM encryption;
- Similar extraction and execution logic. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

These similarities are important because they link the two supply-chain compromises through implementation patterns rather than merely through temporal proximity. They do not, by themselves, prove that every component was developed by the same operators; however, in the context of Mandiant’s direct findings in the 3CX environment, they materially support the conclusion that the same or closely related activity cluster conducted both stages.

Google TAG separately reported that `www.tradingtechnologies[.]com` had been compromised in February 2022 and used to host a hidden iframe associated with a North Korean campaign targeting cryptocurrency services. TAG identified that earlier activity as overlapping with Operation AppleJeus. This does not prove that the website compromise and the later X_TRADER tampering were identical events, but it supplies relevant historical context for the targeting and infrastructure relationship later discussed by Mandiant. ([Google TAG, 2022](https://blog.google/threat-analysis-group/countering-threats-north-korea/))

### 2. 3CX employee workstation compromise

According to Mandiant’s reconstruction, a 3CX employee installed the malicious X_TRADER package on a workstation. The resulting VEILEDSIGNAL infection gave the attacker access to the 3CX environment. The supplied Mandiant evidence does not identify the employee by name, explain why X_TRADER was installed, or establish how the attacker originally modified the Trading Technologies package. Mandiant expressly described the X_TRADER compromise as an earlier supply-chain compromise and stated that the investigation did not determine how many other victims it may have had. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise); [WIRED, 2023](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-times-two))

This limitation matters. The public record supports the conclusion that the X_TRADER package was the initial vector into 3CX, but it does not establish the original intrusion into Trading Technologies. The upstream starting point therefore remains unresolved.

### 3. Credential harvesting and lateral movement inside 3CX

After obtaining access through the compromised workstation, the actor harvested credentials and moved laterally through the 3CX organization. Mandiant identified a compiled version of the open-source **Fast Reverse Proxy** project being used to move laterally. A file named `MsMpEng.exe`, with MD5 `19dbffec4e359a198daf4ffca1ab9165`, was dropped in `C:\Windows\System32`. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

The use of a file named `MsMpEng.exe` is significant because it resembles a legitimate Microsoft Defender executable name and therefore illustrates masquerading or blending with expected system components. Mandiant’s technical annex associates the broader activity with credential access, lateral movement, DLL side-loading, process injection, obfuscation, and ingress tool transfer. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

The public evidence does not provide a complete timeline of every internal host accessed, every credential obtained, or the precise identity of the build servers. It does, however, establish that the intrusion progressed beyond the initial employee workstation and reached the software-development infrastructure.

### 4. Compromise of the Windows and macOS build environments

Mandiant determined that the attacker eventually compromised both the Windows and macOS build environments used by 3CX. On the Windows build environment, the actor deployed **TAXHAUL** and **COLDCAT**. TAXHAUL persisted through DLL search-order hijacking involving the IKEEXT service and ran with LocalSystem privileges. COLDCAT operated as a downloader that generated host identifiers and communicated with actor-controlled infrastructure. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

On the macOS build server, the actor deployed **POOLRAT**, using Launch Daemons as a persistence mechanism. Mandiant clarified that a sample previously described as a potentially new malware family, SIMPLESEA, was in fact POOLRAT. POOLRAT is a macOS backdoor capable of collecting system information, executing commands, reading and writing files, updating configuration, and securely deleting files. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

The compromise of both build environments demonstrates that the actor was not merely attempting to infect individual 3CX users. The attacker sought control over the software-production process itself. That access enabled manipulation of the artifacts distributed to customers.

### 5. Insertion of malware into 3CX DesktopApp installers

The compromised 3CX build environment produced trojanized versions of the legitimate 3CX DesktopApp. Mandiant identified affected versions as 3CX DesktopApp `18.12.416` and earlier. The malicious code included a downloader called **SUDDENICON**, which obtained command-and-control server addresses from encrypted icon files hosted in a GitHub repository. It then downloaded **ICONICSTEALER**, a data-mining component that collected browser information. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

Kaspersky described the same basic execution chain: a malicious DLL within the MSI installer decrypted shellcode from the overlay of `d3dcompiler_47.dll`; the payload extracted command-and-control URLs from icons stored in a GitHub repository; and a downloaded infostealer collected system information and browser history. ([Kaspersky, 2023](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

The Singapore Cyber Security Agency reported that affected Windows Electron versions included `18.12.407` and `18.12.416`, while affected macOS Electron versions included `18.11.1213`, `18.12.402`, `18.12.407`, and `18.12.416`. It stated that the trojanized application could harvest system information and steal data and stored credentials from Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Firefox profiles. ([Cyber Security Agency of Singapore, 2023](https://www.csa.gov.sg/alerts-and-advisories/alerts/al-2023-040/))

### 6. Distribution to the 3CX customer base

The malicious installers were distributed through legitimate 3CX channels and were digitally signed by 3CX, allowing the compromise to reach customers through a trusted software-update mechanism. Early reporting stated that 3CX technology was used by more than 600,000 corporate customers and had more than 12 million active daily users. Huntress reported more than 242,000 publicly exposed 3CX phone-management systems and 2,595 incident reports involving a maliciously hashed `3CXDesktopApp.exe` signed by 3CX on March 13. ([Cybersecurity Dive, 2023](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/))

These figures describe potential exposure or observable infrastructure, not confirmed compromise counts. The evidence should therefore not be interpreted as showing that all 600,000 customers or all 242,000 exposed systems were infected.

## Payloads, victim selection, and operational objective

The initial 3CX payload functioned as a reconnaissance and delivery mechanism. Mandiant identified ICONICSTEALER as a browser-information data miner. Kaspersky reported that the more capable **Gopuram** backdoor was deployed selectively to fewer than ten observed machines. Gopuram supported file-system interaction, process creation, and in-memory modules, including modules for registry manipulation, service management, timestomping, process injection, driver loading, updates, and network or user-management functions. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise); [Kaspersky, 2023](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

Kaspersky observed that the selected victims were particularly associated with cryptocurrency companies, including organizations in Southeast Asia and Western Asia. It described the use of Gopuram as “surgical,” because the backdoor was deployed to fewer than ten systems even though the trojanized 3CX software had a potentially much wider reach. Kaspersky did not report evidence of actual cryptocurrency theft in the victims it observed. ([Kaspersky, 2023](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

Mandiant and WIRED assessed that cryptocurrency theft was likely at least one objective, based on the relationship between Gopuram, AppleJeus, cryptocurrency-focused targeting, CoinGoTrade, JMT Trading, and Trading Technologies. This is an assessment rather than a demonstrated accounting of stolen funds. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise); [WIRED, 2023](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-times-two))

## Attribution analysis

### UNC4736 and North Korean nexus

Mandiant tracks the 3CX activity as **UNC4736**, described as a suspected North Korean nexus cluster. Mandiant assessed with moderate confidence that UNC4736 was related to financially motivated North Korean AppleJeus activity. The assessment relied on malware overlap, infrastructure relationships, and similarities to previous cryptocurrency-focused campaigns. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

### Lazarus and AppleJeus

Kaspersky attributed the deployment of Gopuram to **Lazarus** with medium-to-high confidence. Its reasoning included Gopuram’s coexistence with AppleJeus on a Southeast Asian cryptocurrency company’s systems, shared or related command-and-control infrastructure, the domain `oilycargo[.]com`, and reuse of loader shellcode and the `DllGetClassObject` hashing constant. Kaspersky also cautioned that some loader shellcode was based on open-source code used by other threat actors, meaning the code alone was not uniquely identifying. ([Kaspersky, 2023](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

MITRE ATT&CK identifies AppleJeus as malware used by Lazarus Group and describes Lazarus Group as a North Korean state-sponsored group. It also lists associated names including Labyrinth Chollima, HIDDEN COBRA, ZINC, NICKEL ACADEMY, and Diamond Sleet. MITRE’s description warns that public reporting often uses “Lazarus Group” as an umbrella term for multiple North Korean operators and that shared personnel, infrastructure, malware, and tradecraft make precise attribution difficult. ([MITRE ATT&CK, 2025](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032/); [MITRE ATT&CK, 2025](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0584/))

### Attribution conclusion

The evidence supports the following hierarchy:

1. **Operational cluster:** UNC4736, based on Mandiant’s incident-response tracking.
2. **Broader activity relationship:** financially motivated North Korean AppleJeus activity.
3. **Public umbrella attribution:** Lazarus Group, supported independently by Kaspersky and the MITRE AppleJeus relationship.
4. **Confidence limitation:** the exact organizational identity and internal subdivision remain uncertain.

Some secondary reporting used other labels, including Kimsuky, Emerald Sleet, and Velvet Chollima. Those labels should not be treated as equivalent proof of identity in this case because the supplied Mandiant evidence specifically uses UNC4736 and describes a North Korean nexus, while the supplied Kaspersky evidence uses Lazarus. The discrepancy reflects the broader attribution problem surrounding North Korean operations rather than a basis for asserting that all labels identify the same unit. ([WIRED, 2023](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-times-two); [Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise); [MITRE ATT&CK, 2025](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032/))

## Contradictions and unresolved questions

| Issue | Evidence and interpretation |
|---|---|
| Exact upstream entry into Trading Technologies | Mandiant identified the tampered X_TRADER package but did not determine how Trading Technologies’ software was originally altered. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)) |
| macOS customer activity | Early reporting said activity had been observed on Windows and macOS, while other researchers had not confirmed macOS activity. The CSA advisory nevertheless listed affected macOS versions, and Mandiant confirmed compromise of the macOS build server. This distinguishes macOS build-environment compromise from confirmed end-user execution. ([Cybersecurity Dive, 2023](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/); [Cyber Security Agency of Singapore, 2023](https://www.csa.gov.sg/alerts-and-advisories/alerts/al-2023-040/); [Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)) |
| Final objective | Cryptocurrency theft is a supported assessment, but no supplied source proves that cryptocurrency was stolen from the observed Gopuram victims. ([Kaspersky, 2023](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/)) |
| Actor naming | Mandiant uses UNC4736 and suspected North Korean nexus; Kaspersky uses Lazarus; secondary reporting uses additional labels. The evidence supports relationship, not certainty that all labels denote one precisely defined unit. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise); [Kaspersky, 2023](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/); [MITRE ATT&CK, 2025](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032/)) |

## Conclusion

The public evidence chain is coherent and unusually well supported: a tampered Trading Technologies X_TRADER package compromised a 3CX employee workstation; the attacker used that foothold to harvest credentials and move laterally; the Windows and macOS build environments were compromised; malware was inserted into signed 3CX DesktopApp installers; and the poisoned software was distributed to a large global customer population. The incident therefore represents a confirmed cascading supply-chain compromise rather than an isolated malicious update.

My assessment is that **UNC4736 is the most precise incident-level label**, while **North Korean financially motivated AppleJeus/Lazarus activity** is the most defensible broader public attribution. The technical evidence is stronger than the precise actor naming, and the cryptocurrency-theft objective is plausible and well supported as an assessment, but not proven by the supplied evidence as a completed theft operation.
